title: Rook-pawn special cases

D0.outcome: Explains why the rook pawn draws more often than other pawns: the defending king can sit in the corner, the attacking king has only one side to shelter on, and the edge pawn cannot be supported from both sides; names the exceptions.

D1.outcome: Told the pawn is on the a- or h-file, predicts win or draw in king-and-pawn, king-bishop-and-pawn (by the bishop's colour) and king-knight-and-pawn endings from the defending king's distance to the corner.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled endings tells the rook-pawn draw from the win with a bishop or a knight, using the defending king's distance to the corner, the bishop's colour and the pawn's rank, including the knight-and-pawn-on-the-seventh draw.

D3.outcome: Applies the rook-pawn rule in rook endings (the Lucena bridge fails on the edge) and verifies each claim against the tablebase; predicts what a second pawn or a different bishop changes.

misconceptions: The rook pawn is the weakest pawn, so any ending with it is a draw.
A wrong-coloured bishop always draws, wherever the defending king is.
An extra piece plus a rook pawn always wins.
If a rook-ending technique wins with the b-pawn it wins with the a-pawn.

rating.note: expert estimate; tier=4; every condition has a tablebase-checked instance; the general statements are recalled

conditions: King and rook pawn against king is a draw if the defending king can reach the corner in front of the pawn in time; with the defending king too far from the corner it is a win.

With a bishop, a bishop that controls the pawn's queening square wins in the positions checked; a bishop of the other colour draws when the defending king reaches the corner and wins when that king is cut off from it.

With a knight the extra piece usually wins while the pawn is still on the fourth or fifth rank, even against a king in the corner, but not when the pawn is on the seventh rank and the defending king is shut in the corner in front of it.
In rook endings the rook pawn draws more often because the attacking king cannot build the Lucena bridge on the edge: the arrangement that wins with the b-pawn has a drawn counterpart on the a-file.

contrasts: The same king-and-pawn position with the defending king on d8 instead of a8: the pawn wins.
A wrong-coloured bishop with the defending king cut off far from the corner: there is no wrong-bishop draw, White wins.
Knight and pawn on the seventh against a king in the corner looks like a free win, but it is a draw in the positions probed.
A pawn on the b- to g-file: the corner rule does not apply, and opposition and key squares decide (END.KPK).
